title: Zen, closed
hook: posture, poem, platform, ox, koan, bowl

segments.voice: Yesterday, what Zen is not: not just calm, not just paradox. Your line was more than calm. Which precept did you keep, and where did it pinch? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-four, and the Zen block closes.

Six things on a table. A round cushion. A sheet of paper with a verse brushed on it. A raised wooden seat where a teacher once spoke. A small painting of an ox. A slip of paper with a question on it. And an empty bowl. Each one opened a door in these weeks of Zen and Chan. Today they sit side by side, and then we do the one thing all six keep pointing back to. Today's word, one last time in this block: Zen.
screen: `SIX THINGS ON A TABLE.` → `CUSHION, VERSE, SEAT, OX, QUESTION, BOWL.` → `ZEN.`

segments.voice: Start with the cushion and the verse. The cushion is posture: back upright, hands resting together, eyes lowered, breath allowed to be itself. The verse is the old story of a poem written on a monastery wall, and an answer to it from Huineng, a worker pounding rice in the back, who could not read. Then the seat and the ox. The seat is the platform where Huineng taught, and the sutra named after it: the teaching that the nature to wake up is already here, not somewhere far off. The ox is the set of pictures where a herdsman searches for an ox, finds it, tames it, rides it home, forgets it, and walks back into the market with open hands. Then the question and the bowl. The question is the koan: Zhaozhou's no, three pounds of flax, the cypress in the garden, the stone bridge. A koan is a question you live with, not one you solve over coffee. And the bowl is the formal meal: bowls nested one inside the next, each person taking just enough, and every bowl cleaned at the end. The ordinary task is the practice. Last, what holds all six together. Every one of them comes back to the cushion. The Japanese teacher Dogen called it shikantaza, rendered just sitting. Not sitting to get calm, not sitting to crack a koan. Sitting, as the whole of it. Tomorrow a very different door opens, with a vow, a name and a land of light. Today the block ends where it began, on the cushion.
screen: `THE CUSHION AND THE VERSE.` · `THE SEAT AND THE OX.` · `THE QUESTION AND THE BOWL.` · `ALL SIX COME BACK TO SITTING.` · then, large: `JUST SIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit. That's it. Back upright, hands resting together, eyes lowered or closed. No koan, no counting, no picture to hold. When a thought comes, let it be there and let it go, the way a cloud crosses a window. The bell will hold a short sit now. And if you'd like, come back later today and sit for fifteen minutes the same way, with nothing added. The bell holds the time.
Zen. The Japanese name of the school called Chan in China: posture, verse, platform, ox, koan and bowl, and under all of them, sitting. Today's word.

Your line: just sit. Today, find one moment, on a bus, at a desk, on the edge of the bed, to sit without doing anything else for a few breaths. Then, if you can, the fifteen minutes. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: In Zen communities, zazen, seated meditation, is the center of practice; in the Soto school, the practice Dogen called shikantaza, just sitting, is sitting without a koan or other object.

original.note: Japanese: zen, the reading of the Chinese chan (禪 in traditional characters), the name of the meditation school.

trapdoor: what you thought: zen is a mood.
what it means: a school with a posture, stories, a sutra, pictures, koans and a bowl, all coming back to sitting.
what a scholar hears: Dogen's shikantaza: sitting not as a means to anything, but as the whole of practice.

notes: Block F close: the six objects map the index hook (posture, poem, platform, ox, koan, bowl). The mapping of 'poem' to the wall-verse contest and 'platform' to the Platform Sutra is the writer's reading; confirm against days 1206–1253.
Huineng described as a kitchen worker who could not read: this follows the Platform Sutra's own account; confirm phrasing.
Gateless Gate case 7 paraphrased (Zhaozhou and the bowl); confirm.
Shikantaza attributed to Dogen and glossed as 'just sitting': confirm. Zen/chan reading relationship stated in the original note; confirm characters 禅 / 禪.
Practice invites an optional fifteen-minute sit later (from the outline); the app's sit stays short.
